speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members meet face to face, in this Chamber, to scrutinise legislation and to hold the Government to account.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our rules and procedures, even the architecture of this Chamber, are designed around this function.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But the COVID-19 situation has affected how we work, just as it has affected other parliaments and legislatures around the world.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To ensure the continuity of Parliament, since March, we have been sitting with safe-distancing arrangements.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members are spread out within the Chamber, and some of us are seated at the public galleries.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is about as far as we can go under the law today.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The constitutional provisions governing Parliament are premised on a physical meeting at one place that is appointed by the President.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Certain provisions in the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act are also drafted with reference to Parliament House and its precincts.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But it is entirely conceivable that exigencies may make it unsafe or even impossible for us to meet at one place.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: During such exigencies, it is even more critical for Parliament to carry on its constitutional functions of legislating and holding the Government to account.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have seen the critical role played by this House in the last two months when Members passed the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act as well as the Resilience and Solidarity Budgets.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the constitutional framework, we are an essential service.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The new Article will create a mechanism for Parliament to meet under continuity arrangements.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When the mechanism is activated, Parliament need not meet with all Members gathered at one place.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This physical separation will enhance the survivability of Parliament as an institution.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the context of the COVID-19 situation, separating Members into cohorts and limiting the physical contact between these cohorts allows us to cut down the chance of infection spreading to all Members of Parliament – in other words, the whole of the political leadership of the nation, Government as well as Opposition.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If one cohort is infected, other cohorts can still carry on.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The details of these continuity arrangements will be decided by this House or by you, Mr Speaker.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These details could include allocating Members between the appointed places and the mode of communication between those places.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Continuity arrangements may also involve modifying the existing Standing Orders.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, the rule on ringing division bells would have to be modified if we conduct a division across different locations.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This House or the Speaker would be able to make these modifications.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With these arrangements, Members will be able to take part fully in the proceedings of Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Their presence at an appointed place will count for attendance, quorum and voting purposes.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The powers, immunities and privileges of this House will also be extended to apply to continuity arrangements.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the future, it can be activated by Parliament for six months at a time, if Members consider that it is impossible, unsafe or inexpedient for Parliament to meet in one place.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Parliament can also resolve to deactivate the mechanism at any time.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When the mechanism is deactivated, we will resume normal sittings in this Chamber.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We decided that we do not need to go so far.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore is a small country and Members should be able to travel to alternative sites for Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also wanted Members to be physically and fully present to apply our minds together to the important business of Parliament, even if we co-locate between several places.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As I said when I wrote to Members last Tuesday, there is no immediate need for continuity arrangements.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As the Minister for Health said yesterday, the average number of new cases in the community and unlinked cases have decreased, compared against the week before the circuit breaker was introduced.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This suggests that the circuit breaker measures are effective and so, Mr Speaker, we will continue to meet in this Chamber for this month with safe distancing arrangements.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We hope there will be no need to activate these continuity arrangements.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But we cannot be certain how events will unfold.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Out of an abundance of caution, we should put the constitutional mechanism in place.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If the need arises, for instance, if there is widespread local transmission of COVID-19, we can immediately implement the necessary arrangements.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is why the Bill has been introduced under a Certificate of Urgency.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But let me assure the House that should we decide to meet under continuity arrangements, every Member will be given adequate notice and full technical support.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I would ask for the goodwill of all Members to operate the arrangements if it comes to that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yet the Merdeka Talks two decades later were carried out physically in London over three rounds and two years to determine Singapore's transition from colony to self-governing state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A telephone conference was not considered the best option for such a momentous and delicate negotiation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The question underlying this amendment is not so different from that faced by our pioneers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Can the business of Parliament be conducted properly through technology?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, would permitting the remote meeting of Parliament in multiple places, even during a crisis, fundamentally undermine the quality of decision-making and deliberation conducted by Parliament?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If so, then it may well be better not to meet at all, because the only thing worse than a Parliament unable to conduct business, is one that puts the stamp of legitimacy on decisions that have not been properly debated and deliberated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, on that basis, I support this amendment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I think this amendment speaks to a broader question of how Parliament actually functions, what types of parliamentary work technology helps to enable and what technology still cannot achieve yet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is the foundation of collective decision-making in human societies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But how does Chamber debate actually fulfil that function?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at the actual practice of Parliament, we will see that what we sometimes have is more theatre than debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not mean to insult hon Members in saying so or to doubt their seriousness in coming here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What I mean is that we come prepared knowing that our lines will be put on the Hansard permanently, and reported to a national audience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our true audience often goes beyond the hon Member sitting across from us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The audience is outside the Chamber because Singaporeans need to see that the issues of the day are being debated by the hon Members who represent them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Technology today is well suited to solving the problem of theatre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, there is something lacking when you see a speech online or on TV, as opposed to in person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is why political rallies still draw so many people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But all the basic elements can be brought to us through technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For Chamber debate and Question Time, technology is an excellent substitute for face-to-face meeting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, what does technology struggle with, which is yet vital to the functioning of a Parliament?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think something less appreciated is that much of the work of Parliament is conducted outside the debating Chamber.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And that is because a parliamentary debate is not quite a discussion, negotiation, deliberation or other type of meeting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The rules of parliamentary debate and the knowledge that we are all playing a public role, may constrain us at times from being in real communication with each other.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If the Chamber debate is theatre, then what technology struggles to enable fully is the painstaking backstage work that hon Members carry out every single day – to find out what are the issues affecting Singaporeans, how can the challenges that affect society be solved, what are the ways that we decide as one Singapore to solve them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That work carries on in Parliament as well, but outside this Chamber, in the discussions and meetings that take place during every sitting, and beyond that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Technology is an enabler, but not a leveller, in this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We can certainly email any other hon Member or Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some of us may even feel comfortable calling or video-conferencing a Minister at any time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, when meeting at multiple places, we may not want the set of Members of Parliament at each location to be fixed for the entire duration of the crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even at some risk of cross contamination, it may be useful to have a different set of Members see each other at some interval.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We may also want to create institutions, such as a virtual Members’ Room, so that informal discussions can continue even when we must be apart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And because a constitutional amendment may outlive those of us in the Chamber today, we should also be aware of how it may affect the future business of Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There has been no need since Independence for the Government to collaborate with the Opposition in order to pass parliamentary business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the time may come when the Government does not secure a two-thirds majority, or may even find itself in minority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In that case, having an effective means of building trust and relationships across party lines will be even more important than it is today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, I think it safe to assume that when a Government lacks a majority, Bills do not pass or fail based on the Chamber debate alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The reasons for passage or failure are laid in backroom negotiations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Barring unexpected changes in technology and in social norms, I think this will continue, even though we must all take more care.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is what the Bill refers to as "continuity arrangements".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that is the case – and this is the language used in what will be the new Article 64 – then such arrangements can take effect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The letter sent by the Leader of the House to Members on 27 April regarding this Bill makes clear that the Government believes that there is no immediate need for such continuity arrangements, but that it is appropriate to put this mechanism in place in case the need arises in the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with the Government that it is appropriate to do so now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current COVID-19 pandemic could take a turn for the worse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It behoves us as Members of this House to prepare for that eventuality by putting in place a mechanism now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will devote the remainder of my speech to clarifications and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This practice would appear to be consistent with the language of the new Article 64A(2) since each Member's home could be deemed to be an appointed place and the video-call technology would allow Members to be in contemporaneous communication with one another.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be sure, I am not calling for this to be done now, but the possibility that our COVID-19 situation gets much worse cannot be ruled out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, we cannot rule out the future possibility of an even worse pandemic or some other national security crisis, which would necessitate Members of Parliament calling in from home or other locations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I would like to revisit the issue of live streaming of parliamentary proceedings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When this was discussed in this House in November 2017, the answer given by the Government for why we do not have full live streaming for all Parliament sittings is that it is not in great demand, as based on past experience, only a small fraction of persons would watch certain parliamentary proceedings like the Budget speech live, compared to the number that watch delayed telecasts or clips online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If Parliament adopts continuity arrangements and sits in more than one location, arrangements would need to be made to live stream the proceedings between two or more locations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The investment to do that would need to be made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One can assume that taking the additional step of then making that live stream between the locations available online would be relatively inexpensive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if cost is an impediment, these costs could and should be discussed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I recently had the privilege of moderating a webinar for the Workers' Party Youth Wing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four panellists dialled in from their homes via a video-conferencing service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We were able to live stream the panel discussion on social media, namely Facebook, such that the people who did not sign up to the video-call were still able to watch the panel discussion live on Facebook.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The whole process was relatively simple to run and very cost effective.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many groups and individuals with few resources have live streamed events in this way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we adopt parliamentary continuity arrangements in future, my suggestion is that we could use that as an occasion to experiment with live streaming all parliamentary proceedings under continuity arrangements to the public to test this hypothesis about how much demand there is.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Demand for live streaming may have been low on previous occasions when that was tried, like for certain debates and certain speeches.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if we adopt consistent live streaming of all proceedings, over time, there is the possibility that more people, knowing that this resource is available every time Parliament sits, would use it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this happens, it would be a good thing for our democracy and our society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would probably increase the public knowledge of parliamentary proceedings of how debates turn and how issues are discussed and decided, based on arguments made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This, in turn, is likely to increase the public appetite for participating in the parliamentary process by providing feedback to Members of Parliament, by participating in public debate on issues that are close to their hearts, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, one could argue why can such engagement not happen by the public consuming delayed telecast clips.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Well, for the same reason that there is an audience for live debates, an audience for live political speeches, an audience for live sports and an audience for other kinds of live events, as opposed to there being no audience for such live and real-time events.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The sense of engagement that comes from watching something live and being the first to know is different from watching a delayed clip.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is different from first hearing about something through media reports before you even see the clip.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is a prudent move to ensure that Parliament sittings continue in such unpredictable and challenging times, so that we can still debate and "properly pass the laws and any supplementary funds the Government requires to act in protecting our fellow Singaporeans", as you, Sir, had put it in the last sitting.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, as much as we strive to maintain continuity of Parliament, we must also maintain continuity of access for the public.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, this Bill and its intent in continuity planning is incomplete and creates an unintended dismissal of Singaporeans as part of our parliamentary process.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Public access to Parliament is fundamental to our parliamentary proceedings.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As you shared in your 2018 blog, Mr Speaker, “whatever happens in Parliament affects Singaporeans and Singapore,” so Parliament staying connected to citizens could “bridge knowledge gaps and combat misinformation for a more informed and constructive public discourse on Parliament matters”.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Only with such intentional and on-going engagement can an informed and invested citizenry and therefore a “democracy of deeds” eventuate.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Other than Hansard transcripts and assorted recordings by CNA, the most direct, engaging and intimate access to parliamentary proceedings for members of the public is to watch live from the visitors’ gallery and the press gallery.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I understand that extensive attention was paid to public education of the parliamentary system in the form of galleries on a study trip by the Committee Members during the design of this building in the early 1990s.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, since the introduction of more drastic safe distancing measures, these galleries have been closed to the public and the media.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, the COVID-19 virus has challenged the status quo in so many ways.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The daily updates by the Multi-Ministry Task Force, now live streamed to our homes, has begun to demonstrate the kind of leadership in transparency and accountability away from exceptionalism that has, in my humble opinion, been critical in inspiring the confidence needed in Singaporeans to ride this storm together.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could trust and resilience have been built without risking vulnerability, without risking bad but honest news?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, instead of relying only on media analysis which is constrained by limited air time and print space, Singaporeans should be given live access to parliamentary debates.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow them to be fully invested in the policies deliberated and enacted to tackle this public health and economic crisis.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, you have made admirable efforts in engaging young Singaporeans to take more than a cursory interest in Parliament, Mr Speaker. “My Parliament Journey” allows students to observe the proceedings from the gallery – hordes of them would come in every sitting; I used to enjoy seeing and guessing which school they are from based on their uniform.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly, this live experience is no longer available to them at this time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, I would suggest that in fact, now more than ever, as this Chamber debates Bills and makes laws with urgency to save lives and livelihoods in our biggest crisis since World War II, our young must be engaged to witness history being made and be invested in this “war” that we are fighting together.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Live streaming ensures the continuity of this critical part of their national education and citizenship-building, and provides the opportunity for this to take place at their homes as well.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I would also argue that we must engage in the same way with Singaporeans overseas to enfold them into parliamentary debates to tackle the crisis and our recovery after.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many of my Singaporean friends overseas would have appreciated watching the parliamentary sessions live in the last few sittings as they were so eager to know what the Government would do and what the Members of Parliament would be asking with such a colossal crisis at hand.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Some have been away from Singapore for a while and are seeking ways to stay connected to Singapore in this trying time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is even more important given that elections may be imminent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Having parliamentary live streams will allow Singaporeans abroad to stay connected and is valuable as a long-term measure to help these Singaporeans maintain their stake and commitment to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: COVID-19 has shown us how much of a highly wired world we live in, and live streaming is becoming a way of life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, live streams of parliamentary proceedings are not news sound-bites competing with entertainment channels, they are in fact an investment in our future and our citizenry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And this investment is an investment we must make regardless of viewership, just like how we invested in the generous space for the public and press galleries regardless of visitorship.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But we must also protect the rights of the electorate by continuing to give them direct and live access through live streaming as a continuity arrangement.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can keep distance for safety by closing the public gallery but we must come even closer between the Legislature and our people to forge a stronger compact for a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we have seen in the past few months, it is essential, in these times, that Parliament has the ability to sit and pass the necessary legislation, take swift and decisive fiscal actions, put in place much-needed measures both to control the spread of the virus as well as to alleviate the consequences of these control measures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to discuss these openly and robustly for the sake of the constituents we represent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These make not just for good collaborative democracy where we can get Parliamentary business done efficiently, but such debate allows us to combat fake news and maintain trust and confidence in institutions in this time of crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Faced with a situation, legislative bodies all around the world have asked themselves the question whether they can or need to meet and, if yes, how they will meet.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this COVID-19 crisis, it is only prudent that we possess the ability to be flexible and adjustable as the need requires.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have technology that allows us to do so, and we should be able to make use of it when the need arises, just as many Singapore businesses have had to utilise their continuity plan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, this change from the normal mode of business should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not the norm and should not be the norm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The proposed new Article 64A(2)(b) provides that “arrangements… may be made for Parliament and its committees to sit, meet and despatch business with Members of Parliament being present at two or more appointed places and in contemporaneous communication with one another.” This is not just a change in the way Parliament sits but it will also affect the way Parliament works, and hence should not be utilised lightly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Meeting in a physical place has its role and advantages to democracy that meeting in separate locations cannot replace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By bringing all parliamentarians into one single location, regardless of their political party affiliation or non-partisan affiliation for Nominated Members of Parliament, we as parliamentary colleagues have valuable opportunities to feel the tone and nuance of fellow Members’ speeches.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That adds to our assessment of the subject at hand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What this means is that there is space for persuasion, for close communication, where we can discuss, persuade and work on issues together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not impossible to do so when we do not meet in one single body of caucus, but it is much harder to do so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, while the provisions being suggested today are necessary to address the difficulties of our current times, I would ask humbly that they be leaned on only if absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should quickly try to revert to debating and persuading in a single caucus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What it takes to invoke this arrangement subsequent to the passing of this Bill is a mere majority of Members of Parliament to pass such a resolution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While there will be situations that are clear and uncontroversial such as during this COVID-19 crisis, there may be other times that are less so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Parliament and parliaments in the future who seek to pass such a resolution or sign such a notice should carefully consider the implications of having such an arrangement before doing so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would be especially disadvantageous to parliamentarians with no or smaller natural informal forums to discuss issues with fellow parliamentarians.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand that there is a difference – that we are seeking to amend the Constitution today and the invocation of the provisions in future would not amount to an amendment of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, I would humbly prefer that a two-third majority of sitting members be required to split the caucus into the two or more different locations given the importance of single caucus debates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Leader of the House kindly explain the rationale for requiring a simple majority instead of a super two-third majority?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The ability for the Speaker to present a notice given by Members is good as it provides for a way to invoke these alternative arrangements in a situation where Parliament may not be able to physically meet in one place anymore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During this COVID-19 crisis, it was good that we had a runway – a runway to be able to still meet physically in one place today and pass this piece of legislation that will enable us the flexibility to meet in different places if we need to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We may not have had such an opportunity to do so in the future and having this in the Constitution today, presuming it is passed, is important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, this Bill is broadly drafted so as to accommodate a variety of situations – expected and unexpected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would allow our Parliament and future parliaments the flexibility they may need to handle unexpected and unprecedented crises in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The passing of legislation and robust debates are important features of our democracy and are, in fact, essential.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the shape of the arrangement would probably be informed, to a large extent, by the situation presenting itself at the time, I believe that certain processes and principles, some embedded in our standing orders, are foundational to keeping and maintaining a parliament that is effective and efficient.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another question that I would like to seek clarity on is, constitutionally, how would a newly formed Parliament be able to utilise this continuity plan?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would Members have to first meet physically in one location for the swearing in before these amended provisions can be invoked?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This gives Members the requisite ability to continue to pass legislation needed for the constituents we serve to get through this crisis.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked a few questions about activating the new Article 64A.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, what would amount to inexpedience under the Bill?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is difficult to state a hard and fast rule, because it is impossible to foresee what form an emergency will take and how it would affect Parliament.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It could be a health threat, a virus of another kind, a security threat, or even a natural disaster.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, we need a broadly framed provision to capture all possible scenarios.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But I can say, in principle, we should make every effort to sit in this Chamber, as Mr Christopher de Souza has said convincingly, face-to-face.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We should only move to continuity arrangements in truly exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is because we envisage that the circumstances requiring activation to be those where time and flexibility are of essence.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The situation is likely to be fluid and dynamic, necessitating Parliament to act swiftly in activating the mechanism.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Furthermore, the mechanism does not give the Government or the majority any advantage or put the minority under any disadvantage.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Every Member can still attend, speak and vote from his or her location.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The privileges, immunities and powers of the House will stay the same.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Any matter that requires a supermajority will still require a supermajority.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Given that this is logistical and procedural in nature, there is no reason why we should require a supermajority to activate continuity arrangements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, how would the mechanism be activated by a new Parliament?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Constitutionally, the first item of business for a new Parliament is to elect a Speaker, because Parliament cannot function without a Speaker.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members must also take the Oath of Allegiance.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Only after that can Parliament proceed to transact other business, including activating continuity arrangements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If need be, we can arrange for Members to be divided into cohorts for the purpose of electing a Speaker and taking the Oath.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr de Souza and Ms Anthea Ong asked about the form of continuity arrangements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Bill requires Members in different locations must be in contemporaneous communication with each other.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In principle, we would want a Member who is speaking to be seen and heard live at all locations – so that means a contemporaneous audio-visual link.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members should also be able to ask supplementary questions and seek clarifications, though the process will need to be modified given that we have more than one location.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Speaker should also be seen and heard by all Members.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And there should be certainty on the casting and recording of votes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If the Bill is passed, Parliament Secretariat will look into the procedural, logistical, technical and security details.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Ong and Mr Leon Perera asked about remote participation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Why does the Bill not allow for that?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When a Division is claimed, the bells are rung, and then the Sergeant-at-Arms locks the doors.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When we cast our votes, there are no strangers present, no outside interference.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There is a certain seriousness of purpose, a certain sanctity of process.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And that is true also of what we say and how we debate in this House.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The same solemnity cannot be reproduced in remote proceedings where there is no effective control over the physical environment from which Members dial in.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, in response to Mr Perera's question: whether it is legally possible to have 100 places taking part in a debate; would the Bill allow for remote sitting?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The answer is that it is technically possible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But as I have explained earlier, that is not the scenario that we envisage.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If that had been the case, we would have to put in a lot more certainty, a lot more precautions into how the proceedings would take place in our own individual homes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And that will not make that option comparable to us sitting in this Chamber with the existing procedures.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Remote participation is the only feasible option for legislators who are far away from the seat of the legislature.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But as I said in my opening speech, we are just one city, and Members should have no problems travelling to alternative sites for Parliament sittings.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have therefore struck the balance that is found in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members have called for face-to-face discussions, negotiations and persuasions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, we have tried to incorporate that as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is a balance between considerations of safety, better continuity, but at the same time, keeping as much as possible to the current format of Parliament sittings.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, Members can spread out for continuity purposes, but we also keep the solemnity of a physical meeting.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members also raised some points that fall outside the scope of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With your leave, Sir, I will briefly address them.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Ong and Mr Perera spoke about ensuring the continuity of public access to live parliamentary proceedings, or live streams as they call it, in order to build transparency and trust in times of crisis, to nurture nation building and citizen engagement.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This topic has also been previously discussed in this House.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information, Mr Chee Hong Tat, had explained that the reason why we do not have a live feed.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There are channels available for members of the public, including students and overseas Singaporeans, to easily access full parliamentary proceedings online in a timely, comprehensive and convenient manner.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They can view the complete set of footage of Parliament speeches, as well as questions and answers from each sitting on the CNA Parliament microsite.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In addition, the public has access to the full written record of Parliamentary proceedings via the online Hansard.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And accordingly, to ensure the safety of the public, public viewing from the galleries should only proceed when it is deemed safe to do so.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will be determined as part of the details of the arrangements, to be decided by Mr Speaker or this House.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira spoke about the need for trust and collaboration, even as there are fewer opportunities for Members to meet in person to discuss.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I believe Mr de Souza made a similar point.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I would relay Mr de Souza and Assoc Prof Theseira's concerns to the Parliament Secretariat and ask that they look into giving all Members technical support for continuity in the collaborative engagements between Members, in and outside formal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is critical for us to remain connected and deliberate on critical national issues with each other, as we grapple with the difficult challenges we are faced with.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I trust that my fellow Members will hold fast to our commitment to doing so, even under difficult circumstances.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This way, we will be able to address issues that will matter greatly to the collective well-being of Singaporeans, when it is most needed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a vote is taken to ascertain that the Second Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, which is 61 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will call the names of Members to indicate their votes in the order based on the current seating arrangement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When called upon, Members are to stand up and raise their vote cards in my direction to indicate their votes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is colour-coded but the words are printed there as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will repeat each Member's vote for confirmation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If the vote read is not according to their vote indication, there and then Members should inform me immediately to have their correct vote recorded.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Now, Sir, I beg to move, "That the Bill be now read a Third time."

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "	That the Bill be now read a Third time." That Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a vote is taken to ascertain that the Third Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, which is 61 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will call the names of Members to indicate their votes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When called upon, Members are to stand up and raise the vote cards in my direction to indicate their votes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will repeat each Member's vote for confirmation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If the vote read is not according to their vote indication, Members should inform me immediately to have their correct vote recorded.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Third Reading of the Bill has been carried by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.32 pm until 4.55 pm.
